---
name: entire-orca-workflow
description: Execute the end-to-end GitButler (but) + Entire Trail + multi-agent review + Orca Workspace & GitHub Project Kanban lifecycle (Path B). Use when starting, committing, pushing, opening Trails/PRs, running or triaging `entire review`, or finishing any issue/task in Entire + Orca repositories so no preflight, shadow-PR (`<!-- entire-shadow-pr -->` + `Fixes #N`), review approval, or Kanban step is skipped.
---

# `entire-orca-workflow` — Path B Execution Checklist (GitButler + Entire + Orca)

Repositories using **Path B** split responsibilities cleanly:
- **`AGENTS.md` = Repository Constitution** (domain policies, architecture map, cold-start requirements).
- **`entire-orca-workflow` = Repeatable Execution Engine** (preflight check, 5-phase command checklist, edge-case playbook, and completion gate).

**Never stop after `but push`.** A task is not ready for human merge until all 5 phases below pass `scripts/preflight.mjs --gate in-review`.

---

## Quick Preflight & Completion Gate (`scripts/preflight.mjs`)

Resolve `scripts/preflight.mjs` relative to this skill directory (e.g., `node ~/.pi/agent/skills/entire-orca-workflow/scripts/preflight.mjs` or `node skills/entire-orca-workflow/scripts/preflight.mjs`):

```bash
# 1. Start-of-task cold-start check (auto-detects core vs web-modalities extras)
node ~/.pi/agent/skills/entire-orca-workflow/scripts/preflight.mjs

# 2. End-of-task completion gate (exits non-zero if any Trail, review, PR, Orca, or Kanban step was skipped)
node ~/.pi/agent/skills/entire-orca-workflow/scripts/preflight.mjs \
  --gate in-review \
  --branch <branch> \
  --issue <N>
```

---

## 5-Phase Execution Checklist

### Phase 0: Claim & Dedupe (MANDATORY before spawning a worktree)

Never create a worktree for an issue until you have proven no other agent already claims it.
Two agents once implemented the same fix in parallel (PR #12 and PR #13, Trails #35 and
#37) because both skipped this step. The check turns a silent collision into a fast stop.

1. **Check the shared sources of truth:**
   ```bash
   ISSUE_URL="https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<N>"
   node ~/.pi/agent/skills/entire-orca-workflow/scripts/check-duplicate-work.mjs \
     --issue <N> --repo <owner>/<repo>

   # Human-visible signals:
   gh issue view <N> --repo <owner>/<repo> --json state,assignees,title,url
   gh pr list --repo <owner>/<repo> --state all --search "<N>" \
     --json number,state,headRefName,url
   orca reference find "$ISSUE_URL" --json
   ```
2. **If `check-duplicate-work` exits non-zero (or a PR/worktree/branch already exists):**
   - Do **not** create a new worktree.
   - Resume the existing worktree/branch (see below), or close the duplicate and
     continue on the surviving PR/Trail.
3. **If clear:** assign the issue, mark the board `In Progress`, then create the worktree:
   ```bash
   gh issue edit <N> --repo <owner>/<repo> --add-assignee @me
   gh project item-edit 1 --owner <owner> --url "$ISSUE_URL" \
     --field "Status" --value "In Progress"
   orca worktree create --name <short-kebab-slug> --no-parent \
     --reference "$ISSUE_URL" --json
   ```
4. **Record the claim immediately** so a second agent sees it:
   ```bash
   orca worktree set --worktree active --issue <N> --pr <PR#> \
     --comment "claimed by <agent>" --json
   ```

**Resuming an existing worktree:** run `orca worktree list --json`, find the entry whose
`linkedIssue === <N>` (or whose branch matches the issue title), then `cd` into its `path`
and continue. Do not run `orca worktree create` again.

entire checkpoint list — List checkpoints on the current branch
List checkpoints on the current branch.

By default shows condensed checkpoints from the checkpoints branch for the
current branch. Use --pending for work that is not a checkpoint yet:

  - A preview of the next checkpoint for each session in this worktree with
    pending work. Agent turns are recorded in session state, not in git, so
    this work has no checkpoint ID until you commit it. The preview shows the
    turns since the last checkpoint, the files touched, subagent task records,
    and the prompts since the last checkpoint.
  - Subagent task records of other sessions on HEAD (not yet condensed).
  - Logs-only resume points recovered from commits whose logs are already
    condensed.

Use --outgoing to see what your next 'git push' sends: the checkpoints
queued for the checkpoint sync remote, read from local state with no network
call. Each one shows its ID, age, agent, first prompt (or summary) and the
files it touched. It needs the git-refs checkpoint backend, which pushes one
ref per checkpoint; the git-branch backend pushes entire/checkpoints/v1 as one
branch, so --outgoing reports an error there.

Output modes:
  --json              Machine-readable JSON instead of the human view.
  --pending           Select the pending dataset described above.
  --pending --json    The pending dataset as a JSON array.
  --outgoing          Select the outgoing dataset described above.
  --outgoing --json   The outgoing dataset as one JSON object.

Each --pending --json element has id, message, metadata_dir, date (RFC3339),
is_task_checkpoint, is_logs_only, and when set tool_use_id, condensation_id,
session_id and session_prompt. A next-checkpoint preview element has an empty
id, "is_next_checkpoint": true, and a "next_checkpoint" object:

  {"agent": "...", "turns": 2,
   "files_touched": ["..."],
   "task_records": [{"tool_use_id": "...", "subagent_type": "...",
                     "description": "...", "status": "running|completed"}],
   "prompts": ["..."]}

The arrays are always present, possibly empty.

The --outgoing --json object has checkpoint_push_disabled,
checkpoint_sync_remote, checkpoint_sync_remote_source and
checkpoint_sync_error (as in 'entire status --json'), stale_queue_entries
and a checkpoints array of {checkpoint_id, ref, created_at, agent,
session_count, prompt, summary, files_touched, error}. The array is always
present, possibly empty.

Optionally filter condensed checkpoints by session ID with --session
(not applicable with --pending or --outgoing).

---
Create a commit.

By default, all uncommitted changes of the checkout but runs in are included in the commit: the main
worktree's, or a linked worktree's when run from inside one. This can be controlled with change
flags such as --empty and --interactive, or by providing CHANGES as positional arguments.

Run from a linked worktree, or given changes from one, the commit is placed at the tip of that
worktree's branch. Otherwise, if there are no branches applied, a new branch is created for the
commit. If there is only one stack of branches applied, the commit is placed at the tip of that
stack. Otherwise, the targeting flags --above, --below and --branch control where the commit is
placed. --above and --below are mutually exclusive; combine either with --branch to name a new
branch when targeting a branch.

The commit is expected to have a commit message unless --no-message is provided. If none of 
--no-message, --message or --file is provided, the user's preferred editor is opened to input a
message.

The repository's pre-commit, commit-msg and post-commit hooks run unless --no-hooks is provided. A
failing pre-commit or commit-msg hook aborts the commit.

For more details about CLI IDs, see but help cli-ids.

Usage: but commit [OPTIONS] [CHANGES]...

Arguments:
  [CHANGES]...
          The files or hunks to commit, by CLI ID from but diff or by path.
          
          If omitted, everything uncommitted in the checkout but runs in is committed.

Options:
  -m, --message <MESSAGE>
          The message to use for the commit.
          
          Can be supplied any amount of times, each value being appended to the preceding ones with
          a blank line in between. Without -m, -F or --no-message, a terminal opens the editor and a
          non-interactive run commits with an empty message.

      --no-message
          Create the commit without a message

  -F, --file <FILE>
          Read the commit message from FILE, or from stdin when FILE is -

  -b, --branch [<BRANCH>]
          Place the commit on the branch BRANCH.
          
          With --above or --below, name the new branch created relative to the target branch. The
          name must not already exist; omit it for a generated name. Cannot be combined with commit
          or worktree targets.
          
          Otherwise, if BRANCH does not exist, it is created as an unstacked branch. If BRANCH is
          omitted, an unstacked branch with a generated name is created.
          
          If BRANCH is a worktree or a branch checked out in one, the commit is placed on the tip of
          that worktree's branch.
          
          Run from a linked worktree with a detached HEAD, a new BRANCH starts at that HEAD and is
          checked out there before the commit is placed on it.

Update applied branches and worktrees onto the latest target.

This fetches the latest changes from the remote and rebases all applied branches and linked
worktrees on top of the updated target branch.

When the target branch has no upstream, for example in a repository without a remote, there is
nothing to fetch: this updates the branches onto the local target branch instead, for example after
merging branches into main with git merge.

You should run this regularly to keep your branches up to date with the latest changes from the main
development line.

You can run but pull --check first to see if your branches can be cleanly merged into the target
branch before running the update.

Commits pushed to a branch's own remote counterpart are not integrated by pull; use but branch
update <branch> for those.
